questions.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $U$ and $V$ above. Let $X$ be a $2\times 3$ standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $X,$ what is the third principal component of the data?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>{\lambda }_{3}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- the $3$rd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to the $3$rd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}.$

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $3\times 3$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and

- $V$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the third principal component is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $V$ is a $m\times m$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the second principal component is ${v}_{2}.$

questions.problem:
A scientist measured $5$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{5},$ for each athlete among a group of athletes. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular athlete.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=5,\,{\sigma }_{2}=2,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.5,\,{\sigma }_{5}=0.1.
$$

The scientist then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{2},$ where ${V}_{2}$ is the $5\times 2$ matrix consisting of the first two principal components of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},…,{\sigma }_{5}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(5)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(0.5)^{2}+(0.1)^{2} \\  & =30.26\end{aligned}
$$

Since the scientist used only the first two principal components, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(5)^{2}+(2)^{2} \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{29}{30.26} \\  & ≈0.958 \\  & =95.8%.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
An epidemiologist measured $4$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4},$ for each disease affecting a specific population. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular individual.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=11,\,{\sigma }_{2}=7,\,{\sigma }_{3}=5,\,{\sigma }_{4}=2.
$$

The epidemiologist then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{1},$ where ${V}_{1}$ is the $4\times 1$ matrix consisting of the first principal component of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{4}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},{y}_{4}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},{\sigma }_{3}^{2},{\sigma }_{4}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},{y}_{4}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(11)^{2}+(7)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(2)^{2} \\  & =199\end{aligned}
$$

Since the epidemiologist used only the first principal component, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(11)^{2} \\  & =121.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{121}{199} \\  & ≈0.608 \\  & =60.8%.\end{aligned}
$$
